primaryText: Anna čitaet knigu
comment: Both readings available without articles: the shifts iota and ex do the work.

primaryText: John is tall, handsome and the love of my life.
comment: A definite coordinates with predicative adjectives.

primaryText: The love of my life is tall, handsome, and John.
comment: A proper name does not.

primaryText: John considers this woman the queen of the world.

alternatives.form: John considers this woman a good teacher.
John considers this woman his girlfriend.
John considers this woman some particular queen.

comment: Printed as (5a) with the acceptable fillers braced and (5b) with the starred ones: consider selects predicates, which definite, indefinite and possessive descriptions and adjectives supply, and names, some-indefinites and pronouns do not.

primaryText: A great man and a good father has passed away.
comment: Singular agreement: the conjunction describes one individual. Winter credits the examples to Hoeksema (1988: 36).

primaryText: My great opponent and the hero of my youth has passed away.
comment: Winter credits the examples to Hoeksema (1988: 36).

primaryText: A great man and the best magician in New Jersey has passed away.
comment: Winter credits the examples to Hoeksema (1988: 36).

primaryText: Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde have passed away.

alternatives.form: Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde has passed away.

comment: Printed as have/*has: proper names do not participate in appositional conjunction even when co-referential.

primaryText: Some great man and some good father have passed away.

alternatives.form: Some great man and some good father has passed away.

comment: Printed as have/*has: some-indefinites do not participate either.

primaryText: He's not the ambassador to Spain—there are two.
comment: Infelicitous without heavy stress on the: uniqueness is not targetable by ordinary negation, against the Russellian entry (52a).

primaryText: There are two ambassadors to Spain; therefore, he is not the ambassador to Spain.
comment: Infelicitous without heavy stress on the.

primaryText: I know that this is at least one of the reasons. Is it the reason?
discourseSegments: I know that this is at least one of the reasons.
Is it the reason?
comment: The is not interchangeable with the only, against the Russellian entry, on which the two coincide.

primaryText: I know that this is at least one of the reasons. Is it the only reason?
discourseSegments: I know that this is at least one of the reasons.
Is it the only reason?
comment: The only P satisfies weak uniqueness trivially, so the presupposition of the is met.

primaryText: The greatest French soldier is the king of France.
comment: Predicted simply false on the predicative reading: predicative definites presuppose no existence.

primaryText: The king of France is the greatest French soldier.
comment: Predicted to lack a truth value: the argumental definite is determinate and presupposes existence; the paper finds the contrast with (13) subtle.

primaryText: Scott is the only author of Waverley.
comment: Implies that there is one author of Waverley.

primaryText: Scott is not the only author of Waverley.
comment: The anti-uniqueness effect: the most prominent interpretation has more than one author, so no existence presupposition for the only author, (64).

primaryText: Is Scott the only author of Waverley?
comment: There may be multiple authors.

primaryText: If Scott is the only author of Waverley, then…
comment: There may be multiple authors.

primaryText: You're not the queen of the world.
comment: No commitment to a queen of the world.

primaryText: Seven is not the largest prime number.
comment: No commitment to a largest prime number; superlatives lack only's inference pattern.

primaryText: Lack of supply is not the sole cause of Britain's housing crisis.
comment: Naturally occurring; sole patterns with only.

primaryText: Search engine optimization is not the single thing to think about with regards to search engine ranking.
comment: Naturally occurring; single patterns with only.

primaryText: It is worthwhile to visit Kuala Lumpur to see the future of modern Asia, but it is not the one reason to visit.
comment: Naturally occurring; one patterns with only.

primaryText: Dean Hall doesn't have the exclusive right to open-world multiplayer zombie apocalypse simulators, you know.
comment: Naturally occurring: Dean Hall has the right and so do others, so the exclusive right does not exist.

primaryText: The golden mountain does not exist.
comment: Felt to be true: no narrow existence presupposition.

primaryText: Max wanted a train set for Christmas but when he opened his presents, the train set wasn't there.
comment: Adapted by the paper from Cooper (1978): the description picks out no actual object.

primaryText: I forgot to buy the wine.
comment: Due to Robin Cooper, p.c.

primaryText: We cancelled the May meeting.
Captain James Cook finally disproved the existence of the Northwest Passage in 1778.
Sue and Jane both scored goals, so Jane didn't score the only goal. It wasn't a bicycle-kick, either.
discourseSegments: Sue and Jane both scored goals, so Jane didn't score the only goal.
It wasn't a bicycle-kick, either.
comment: The only goal is no antecedent for it: broad existence fails under anti-uniqueness.

primaryText: Max wanted a train set for Christmas but when he opened his presents, the train set wasn't there. His parents had forgotten to buy it.
discourseSegments: Max wanted a train set for Christmas but when he opened his presents, the train set wasn't there.
His parents had forgotten to buy it.
comment: The train set antecedes it though it lacks narrow existence.

primaryText: We cancelled the May meeting. It was deemed unnecessary.
discourseSegments: We cancelled the May meeting.
It was deemed unnecessary.

primaryText: Captain James Cook disproved the existence of the Northwest Passage in 1778. It was not included on maps after that.
discourseSegments: Captain James Cook disproved the existence of the Northwest Passage in 1778.
It was not included on maps after that.

primaryText: A: Sam is looking for the train set. B: Which train set? A: The one he was promised for Christmas.
discourseSegments: A: Sam is looking for the train set.
B: Which train set?
A: The one he was promised for Christmas.
comment: Cooper's dialogue, coherent with no particular train set promised: the which question diagnoses broad existence.

primaryText: A: Sue and Jane both scored goals, so Jane didn't score the only goal. B: Which goal?
discourseSegments: A: Sue and Jane both scored goals, so Jane didn't score the only goal.
B: Which goal?
comment: The only goal has no broad existence presupposition.

primaryText: I don't consider Scott the only author of Waverley.
comment: Under consider, which selects a predicate, no equative-like reading with a presupposed unique author is available.

primaryText: He is neither handsome nor the only man you'll ever meet.
comment: No reading presupposing exactly one man the addressee will meet.

primaryText: Mary is neither stupid nor the only person to have made this mistake.
Meanwhile, the Enterprise computer has fallen in love with Captain Kirk and considers him the only person in the universe.
comment: Naturally occurring: no implication that exactly one person is in the universe, with no global inconsistency to force local accommodation.

primaryText: One political wag characterized him as the only man in America who could get away with wearing a toga.
comment: Naturally occurring.

primaryText: THE king of France does not exist—there are two.

alternatives.form: The king of France does not exist—there are two.

comment: Printed as {THE/#The}: stress makes uniqueness at issue.

primaryText: THE man who can best her in a battle of wits does not exist—there are two.

alternatives.form: The man who can best her in a battle of wits does not exist—there are two.

comment: Printed as {THE/#The}.

primaryText: I don't know whether iguanas have hearts, but is that the heart?
context: An iguana has been dissected and an observer points to an unidentified part.
comment: Felicitous under the assumption that iguanas have only one heart if any.

primaryText: I don't know whether iguanas have bones, but is that the bone?
context: An iguana has been dissected and an observer points to an unidentified part.
comment: Infelicitous under the assumption that iguanas have multiple bones if any.

primaryText: That's definitely not the heart. Iguanas don't have hearts.
discourseSegments: That's definitely not the heart.
Iguanas don't have hearts.
context: An iguana has been dissected and an observer points to an unidentified part.
comment: Uniqueness without existence under negation.

primaryText: That's definitely not the bone. Iguanas don't have bones.
discourseSegments: That's definitely not the bone.
Iguanas don't have bones.
context: An iguana has been dissected and an observer points to an unidentified part.
comment: The mass reading of bone that can rescue (46b) is less accessible here, where the plural bones also occurs (fn. 17).

primaryText: If that's the heart, then this must be a blood vessel.
context: An iguana has been dissected and an observer points to an unidentified part.
comment: The uniqueness presupposition projects from the antecedent of a conditional.

primaryText: If that's the bone, then this must be a tendon.
context: An iguana has been dissected and an observer points to an unidentified part.
comment: May become felicitous with bone understood as a mass term (fn. 17).

primaryText: The baby's fully developed hand wrapped itself around the finger of the surgeon.
comment: Barker's possessive weak definite, accompanied by a picture of the surgeon with all ten fingers; the paper defers to an alternative mode of composition.

primaryText: The baby's fully developed hand wrapped itself around the finger of the surgeon's.
comment: The double genitive variant is unacceptable.

primaryText: He is standing at the corner of the intersection.
comment: Intersections have four corners.

primaryText: John and Mary are exactly zero friends of mine.
comment: Winter's example: the be shift would give it a coherent reading, so the predicative case is taken as basic instead. Winter (p. 144) marks it *; the paper reprints it with #.

primaryText: Scott is the only author of Waverley.

alternatives.form: Scott is an only author of Waverley.

comment: Printed as {the/*an}: the indefinite is blocked by Maximize Presupposition, since the only P satisfies weak uniqueness.

primaryText: In China it is common for every student in a class to be an only child.
comment: An only child is licensed because only child, read relationally, lacks weak uniqueness.

primaryText: Over the past 29 years, I've tried to contact everyone I can around the world who's been an only survivor of a large plane crash.
comment: Naturally occurring, after an archetype pointed out by Roger Levy: the crash scopes inside the description (69), which then holds of as many individuals as there are crashes with a single survivor, so the is not licensed on that derivation.

primaryText: I don't know how many books Frida has written. But as it happens, I'm now reading a book she wrote.
discourseSegments: I don't know how many books Frida has written.
But as it happens, I'm now reading a book she wrote.

alternatives.form: I don't know how many books Frida has written. But as it happens, I'm now reading the book she wrote.

comment: Printed as (a/#the): the context leaves uniqueness open, so the definite's update is undefined and the indefinite is not blocked.

primaryText: Frida has written exactly one book. But as it happens, I'm now reading the book she wrote.
discourseSegments: Frida has written exactly one book.
But as it happens, I'm now reading the book she wrote.

alternatives.form: Frida has written exactly one book. But as it happens, I'm now reading a book she wrote.

comment: Printed as (#a/the): after the first sentence every world of the context has exactly one book, both updates coincide, and the definite blocks the indefinite.

primaryText: It's possible that the ghost in Hans's attic is being noisy.
comment: Elbourne's objection to the Russellian analysis: commits the speaker to a ghost, unlike (76b), so the two are not equivalent.

primaryText: It's possible that there is exactly one ghost in Hans's attic and it is being noisy.
Chris saw the (only) invited talk.
comment: Implies exactly one invited talk.

primaryText: Chris didn't see the (only) invited talk.
comment: Still implies exactly one invited talk: existence and uniqueness presupposed.

primaryText: That was the only invited talk.
comment: Affirms that there was a single invited talk.

primaryText: That wasn't the only invited talk.
comment: Does not imply a single invited talk.

primaryText: Chris saw an invited talk.
comment: Implies at least one invited talk.

primaryText: Chris didn't see an invited talk.
comment: No entailment that there were any invited talks.

primaryText: Anna didn't give the only invited talk.
comment: Anti-uniqueness reading: more than one invited talk, one of which Anna gave; determinate reading: exactly one, which Anna did not give. With nuclear stress on only, only the former, (99).

primaryText: Anna didn't see the only invited talk.
comment: Implies exactly one invited talk; the anti-uniqueness reading becomes at least marginally available with nuclear stress on only, (99).

primaryText: Mary didn't score the only goal.
Mary didn't cheer for the only goal.
comment: Implies exactly one goal.

primaryText: Mary didn't bring the only chocolate cake.
Mary didn't taste the only chocolate cake.
Mary didn't have the only beautiful dress there.
Mary didn't admire the only beautiful dress there.
Every student saw a long film with Marlene Dietrich in it.
comment: The indefinite under every has only the indeterminate reading: had uniqueness held in the context, the would have been used.

primaryText: It's possible that the grandfather clock in Hans's attic is making a noise.
comment: Suggests the speaker takes there to be a grandfather clock in the attic: the iota reading is preferred by Type Simplicity.

primaryText: It's possible that there is a grandfather clock in Hans's attic and it is making a noise.
comment: Does not.

primaryText: Mary didn't write the only decent paper.
comment: A verb of creation: implies multiple decent papers.

primaryText: Mary didn't read the only decent paper.
comment: Not a verb of creation: no anti-uniqueness reading absent supporting context.

primaryText: There are at least seven cakes. If Maria brings a cake, that will make eight.
discourseSegments: There are at least seven cakes.
If Maria brings a cake, that will make eight.
comment: The arithmetic inference is felicitous: the verb introduces entities.

primaryText: There are at least seven cakes. If Maria takes a cake, that will make eight.
discourseSegments: There are at least seven cakes.
If Maria takes a cake, that will make eight.
comment: The arithmetic inference is infelicitous: the verb does not introduce entities.

primaryText: There are at least seven books. If Maria writes a book, that will make eight.
discourseSegments: There are at least seven books.
If Maria writes a book, that will make eight.
comment: The arithmetic inference is felicitous: the verb introduces entities.

primaryText: There are at least seven books. If Maria reads a book, that will make eight.
discourseSegments: There are at least seven books.
If Maria reads a book, that will make eight.
comment: The arithmetic inference is infelicitous: the verb does not introduce entities.

primaryText: There have been at least seven strapless dresses on the runway. If Maria wears a strapless dress, that will make eight.
discourseSegments: There have been at least seven strapless dresses on the runway.
If Maria wears a strapless dress, that will make eight.
comment: The arithmetic inference is felicitous: the verb introduces entities.

primaryText: There have been at least seven strapless dresses on the runway. If Maria likes a strapless dress, that will make eight.
discourseSegments: There have been at least seven strapless dresses on the runway.
If Maria likes a strapless dress, that will make eight.
comment: The arithmetic inference is infelicitous: the verb does not introduce entities.

primaryText: There are at least seven BMWs in the neighborhood. If Maria has a BMW, that will make eight.
discourseSegments: There are at least seven BMWs in the neighborhood.
If Maria has a BMW, that will make eight.
comment: The arithmetic inference is felicitous: the verb introduces entities.

primaryText: There are at least seven BMWs in the neighborhood. If Maria cleans a BMW, that will make eight.
discourseSegments: There are at least seven BMWs in the neighborhood.
If Maria cleans a BMW, that will make eight.
comment: The arithmetic inference is infelicitous: the verb does not introduce entities.

primaryText: Nobody baked any brownies. Some of them are made with nuts.
discourseSegments: Nobody baked any brownies.
Some of them are made with nuts.
comment: Under negation an entity-introducing verb leaves no existence implication for its indefinite object, so the anaphor fails.

primaryText: Nobody tasted any brownies. Some of them are made with nuts.
discourseSegments: Nobody tasted any brownies.
Some of them are made with nuts.
comment: For other verbs the existence implication survives negation.

primaryText: Nobody painted any pictures. They were landscapes.
discourseSegments: Nobody painted any pictures.
They were landscapes.
comment: Under negation an entity-introducing verb leaves no existence implication for its indefinite object, so the anaphor fails.

primaryText: Nobody disliked any pictures. They were landscapes.
discourseSegments: Nobody disliked any pictures.
They were landscapes.
comment: For other verbs the existence implication survives negation.

primaryText: Nobody found any foreign cars. All of them were made in Italy.
discourseSegments: Nobody found any foreign cars.
All of them were made in Italy.
comment: Under negation an entity-introducing verb leaves no existence implication for its indefinite object, so the anaphor fails.

primaryText: Nobody scratched any foreign cars. All of them were made in Italy.
discourseSegments: Nobody scratched any foreign cars.
All of them were made in Italy.
comment: For other verbs the existence implication survives negation.

primaryText: Nobody ran any businesses. They were well-established and profitable.
discourseSegments: Nobody ran any businesses.
They were well-established and profitable.
comment: Under negation an entity-introducing verb leaves no existence implication for its indefinite object, so the anaphor fails.

primaryText: Nobody opposed any businesses. They were well-established and profitable.
discourseSegments: Nobody opposed any businesses.
They were well-established and profitable.
comment: For other verbs the existence implication survives negation.

primaryText: If John sees a sparrow, that will make eight.
context: A bird-watching expedition in which the participants are keeping track of how many birds have been seen.
comment: See is entity-introducing in this frame.

primaryText: He indeed saw that sparrow. But he didn't see the only sparrow—Sue had seen another one earlier!
discourseSegments: He indeed saw that sparrow.
But he didn't see the only sparrow—Sue had seen another one earlier!
comment: Due to a reviewer: anti-uniqueness with see in its entity-introducing sense.

primaryText: Mary's pet rabbit is in the cage and Mary's pet rabbit is outside the cage.
comment: Löbner's negation test: an argumental possessive with a definite possessor behaves as a term.

primaryText: Some rabbit is in the cage and some rabbit is outside the cage.
Mary's pet rabbit is from South Africa and Mary's pet rabbit is a secret agent.
comment: Equivalent to: Mary's pet rabbit is a secret agent from South Africa.

primaryText: Some rabbit is from South Africa and some rabbit is a secret agent.
comment: Not equivalent to: Some rabbit is a secret agent from South Africa.

primaryText: The rabbit in the cage is Mary's pet and the rabbit sitting just outside the cage is Mary's pet.
comment: Predicative possessives pattern with predicative indefinites, not definites: no uniqueness requirement.

primaryText: The rabbit in the cage is a pet Mary owns and the rabbit sitting just outside the cage is a pet Mary owns.
The rabbit in the cage is the pet Mary owns and the rabbit sitting just outside the cage is the pet Mary owns.
The rabbit from South Africa is Mary's pet and the Indonesian cat is Mary's pet.
comment: Not equivalent to: Mary has a South African pet rabbit which is also an Indonesian cat.

primaryText: The rabbit from South Africa is a pet Mary owns and the Indonesian cat is a pet Mary owns.
comment: Not equivalent to: Mary has a South African pet rabbit which is also an Indonesian cat.

primaryText: The rabbit from South Africa is the pet Mary owns and the Indonesian cat is the pet Mary owns.
comment: Equivalent to: Mary has a South African pet rabbit which is also an Indonesian cat.

primaryText: Is that your bicycle?
comment: Does not presuppose that the hearer has only one bicycle: (117) is a felicitous reply.

primaryText: Is that the bicycle you own?
comment: (117) would not be a felicitous reply.

primaryText: Yes, and that one there is also mine.
comment: A reply to (116a) but not to (116b).

primaryText: This is the state's property, and so is that.
This is the property that the state owns, and so is that.
This is Jane's work, and so is that.
This is the work that Jane did, and so is that.
Trotsky is 100% the king's horse.
comment: Printed as {the king's horse/#Superman}: the modifier excludes the equative reading, and the king may have several horses.

primaryText: Trotsky is to some extent the king's horse.

alternatives.form: Trotsky is to some extent Superman.

comment: Printed as {the king's horse/#Superman}.

primaryText: He is tall, dark, handsome, and my cousin (alas!).
comment: The speaker may have several cousins.

primaryText: I consider this your problem.
comment: Does not convey that the addressee has only one problem.

primaryText: I consider this the problem you have.
comment: Conveys that the addressee has only one problem.

primaryText: That wasn't John's only contribution.
comment: Predicative possessives show anti-uniqueness, so they presuppose no existence.

primaryText: That wasn't Mary's fault!
comment: Does not imply that anything was Mary's fault.

primaryText: A: Is that your eighteen-wheeler that's blocking the entrance? B: No!
discourseSegments: A: Is that your eighteen-wheeler that's blocking the entrance?
B: No!
comment: Does not imply that speaker B owns an eighteen-wheeler.

primaryText: Green card holders don't just take from the USA, nor do they make their only contribution through taxes.
comment: Attested: an argumental possessive with an indeterminate reading; the paper analyses the parallel (132) in (133)–(134).

primaryText: The Grinch didn't make his only appearance when he attempted to steal Christmas. Dr. Seuss reprised the character in two more books: …
discourseSegments: The Grinch didn't make his only appearance when he attempted to steal Christmas.
Dr. Seuss reprised the character in two more books: …
comment: Attested: analysed as (133)–(134) with ex over the possessive.

primaryText: Rajka nije bila jedini predavač: Megan je isto održala predavanje.
translation: Rajka was not the only speaker: Megan also gave a talk
comment: Croatian, for which the paper thanks Rajka Smiljanic: a bare nominal with the indeterminate reading that the only speaker has in English.
